1 · Why containers

Life before containers

People installed databases, runtimes and tools directly on each machine. It worked — until it did not.

⚙

Different OSes

MongoDB, Redis, MySQL, Node, Python — each with different install steps and paths per OS.

☰

Long checklists

Ten-step install guides. Every step is a place where something silently goes wrong.

❄

“Snowflake” servers

Servers configured by hand. No two are identical, and nobody remembers why.

📄

Deployment = a text guide

The deploy process lives in a wiki page. Easy to misread, easier to skip a step.

⚡

Dependency conflicts

Two apps on one host need two different versions of the same library. Someone loses.

💬

Dev ↔ Ops mismatch

“I thought Redis was 6.x on prod.” The environments drifted apart months ago.

1 · Why containers

Traditional deployment, in detail

One machine, one OS, one shared library tree — every app is a tenant fighting for the same files.

How it worked
  • Install the runtime, the database and every library directly on the host.
  • Configuration lives in /etc, in someone’s shell history, and in a wiki page.
  • Deploying a new version = SSH in, pull code, restart the service, hope.
⚠
The classic break Two apps on one server need Python 3.8 and Python 3.11. There is exactly one /usr/bin/python3. Someone has to lose.

1 · Why containers

Virtual machines: isolation, at a cost

VMs solved the conflict problem — by giving every app its own machine, virtually.

What a hypervisor does
  • Emulates virtual hardware: CPU, disk, NIC, memory.
  • Each VM boots a complete guest operating system — its own kernel.
  • Isolation is very strong: a kernel panic in one guest does not touch the others.
⚠
The cost You pay for that isolation in disk (GBs per VM), RAM (a whole OS resident) and boot time (minutes).

1 · Why containers

Containers: share the kernel, isolate the process

A container is not a small VM. It is a normal Linux process that has been lied to about what it can see.

What the kernel provides
  • Namespaces — each container gets its own view of PIDs, mounts, network interfaces, hostname and users.
  • cgroups — limits and accounts for CPU, memory, and I/O per container.
  • No emulated hardware, no second kernel — just isolated processes on the host kernel.
⚠
The one catch Containers still need a compatible kernel. Linux containers run on Linux; on macOS and Windows, Docker Desktop quietly runs them inside a Linux VM.

1 · Why containers

Side by side: VM vs container

Both are valid tools. In practice, containers run inside cloud VMs — you use both.

Virtual MachineContainer
Isolation unitA whole virtual machine with its own kernelA process group with its own namespaces
Guest OSRequired — one full OS per VMNone — shares the host kernel
Size on diskGigabytes (OS + app)Megabytes (depends on the base image)
Startup timeUsually minutes — a full bootUsually seconds — just process start
Isolation strengthVery strong — hardware-level boundaryStrong, but kernel is shared — a kernel bug is a shared risk
PortabilityMove a disk image; heavy, hypervisor-specificSame image on any host with a compatible runtime (and matching CPU architecture, unless multi-arch)
Good forDifferent OSes, strict tenancy, legacy workloadsAlmost every modern app, CI, and microservices

1 · Why containers

So: what is a container? What is Docker?

Two different words that students constantly merge. Keep them apart.

Container — the concept

A standardised way to package an application together with its dependencies and configuration, so it runs the same way on a laptop, a CI server, or in production.

one artifactsame everywhereno install guide
Docker — the product

A platform built around that idea: build images, run containers, push/pull from registries, and hand off to an orchestrator (Kubernetes or Swarm) when one machine is not enough.

buildrunpush / pullorchestrate

1 · Why containers

The mental shift

Containers separate “what the app needs” from “what the machine already has”.

What the app needs

Runtime, libraries, system packages, config defaults.

Lives inside the image. You control it, you version it, you ship it.

What the machine has

A kernel and a container runtime. Almost nothing else.

Servers become interchangeable. Rebuilding one is not an event.

IdeaIn plain language
Portable artifactYou ship a known-good bundle instead of a long install document.
Efficient dev & deployThe same image in dev, staging and prod removes most “works on my machine” problems.
★
After containers Teams now collaborate on a buildable artifact. Runtime configuration on the server gets smaller, and far more repeatable.

2 · Objects

The five Docker objects

Every command you will type today is docker <object> <sub-command> against one of these five.

▤

Images

Read-only templates. Built from a Dockerfile, made of stacked layers, identified by name:tag.

◉

Containers

Running (or stopped) instances of an image, with a thin writable layer on top.

⇄

Networks

How containers reach each other and the outside world. bridge, host, none.

◫

Volumes

Storage that outlives the container. Named volumes, bind mounts, tmpfs.

☁

Registry

Where images are stored and shared. Docker Hub, ECR, ACR, GCR, GHCR.

Image vs container — the critical distinction

Image is to container what a class is to an object, or a recipe to a meal.

Image — the blueprint
nginx:1.25-alpine
read-only · layered · ~23 MB

Built once. Tagged. Pushed to a registry. Pulled by anyone.
Nothing runs. It is a recipe on a shelf.

⟶
docker run
one image,
many containers
Containers — the running instances
web-1
running · :8080
web-2
running · :8081
web-3
exited (0)

Each has its own writable layer, its own PID, its own IP, its own logs.
Delete one — the image is untouched.

2 · Objects

Layers: how an image is actually built

This one diagram explains image size, build cache, and why container data disappears.

One image = a stack of read-only layers
rwContainer writable layerephemeral
L5CMD ["node","server.js"]0 B
L4COPY . .1.2 MB
L3RUN npm ci48 MB
L2COPY package*.json ./4 KB
L1FROM node:20-alpine130 MB
  • Each Dockerfile instruction that changes the filesystem creates a new layer.
  • Layers are immutable and shared. Ten containers from one image store the read-only layers once.
  • Starting a container just adds a thin writable layer on top — that is why it takes milliseconds.
  • Writes go to that top layer (copy-on-write) and are deleted with the container.
★
Why order matters Change one line in your source and only L4 and above rebuild. That is why COPY package*.json comes before COPY . . — we protect the expensive npm ci layer from the cache.
Docker · ITI DevOps 202620 / 140
2 · Objects

The one-minute mental model

If you remember nothing else, remember this loop.

  1. 1
    Find or build an image — from a registry, a Dockerfile, or your CI pipeline.
  2. 2
    docker pull — only needed if the image is remote and not cached locally. docker run does it for you automatically.
  3. 3
    docker run — creates and starts a container from that image.
  4. 4
    Ports, volumes and networks — connect the container to the outside world and to persistent data.
  5. 5
    docker logs / docker exec — your first two tools when something goes wrong.
★
Ninety percent of daily Docker use is these five steps. Everything else in this deck is detail hanging off them.

Inside the Docker Engine

The CLI is a client. Everything real happens in the daemon and below.

The stack, top to bottom
Docker CLI what you type
↓REST API over a unix socket
Docker Daemon dockerd
↓
containerd container lifecycle
↓
containerd-shim one per container
↓
runC OCI runtime
↓
libcontainer
↓
Namespaces & cgroups Linux kernel
ComponentResponsibility
Docker CLIWhat you type. An API client — it runs nothing itself.
Docker Daemon
dockerd		The long-running service. Owns images, networks, volumes and builds.
containerdSupervises the container lifecycle: pull, unpack, start, stop.
containerd-shimOne tiny process per container. Survives daemon restarts.
runCThe OCI runtime. Spawns the process, then exits.
libcontainerThe library runC uses to reach kernel primitives.
Namespaces & cgroupsThe kernel features that do the actual isolating.
Docker · ITI DevOps 202626 / 140
3 · Engine

Namespaces and cgroups: the two kernel features

These are ordinary Linux kernel features. Docker did not invent them — it made them usable.

Namespaces — what a process can SEE
pid

Process IDs

Your app is PID 1 inside; the host sees a different number.

net

Network stack

Its own interfaces, IP, routing table and ports.

mnt

Mount points

Its own root filesystem view — the image layers.

uts

Hostname

Its own hostname, set with --hostname.

ipc

Shared memory

Isolated System V IPC and POSIX queues.

user

UID / GID mapping

Root in the container can be a normal user on the host.

cgroups — what a process can USE
⚙

CPU

Shares, quotas and pinning. --cpus, --cpuset-cpus.

◫

Memory

Hard limits. Exceed it and the kernel OOM-kills the container.

⇅

Block I/O

Read/write throughput and IOPS ceilings per device.

⋮

PIDs

Caps the number of processes — stops fork bombs.

★
Namespaces isolate. cgroups limit. Together they turn an ordinary process into what we call a container — no virtual hardware anywhere.

Verifying the installation

Three commands that look similar and answer very different questions.

bash
docker version
ⓘ
Full client and server version info. If the Server block is missing, the daemon is not running or you cannot reach the socket.
bash
docker --version
ⓘ
Just the CLI version, one line. Handy in scripts and CI checks.
bash
docker system info
★
Storage driver, cgroup version, image and container counts, registry mirrors, warnings. First stop when something behaves strangely.

Managing the Docker service

systemd (Linux)
bash
systemctl start docker
bash
systemctl status docker
bash
systemctl stop docker
What you are actually controlling
ⓘ
These commands control dockerd — the daemon in the middle of the stack we just drew. Stop it and the CLI immediately loses its API.
⚠
The error you will see Cannot connect to the Docker daemon at unix:///var/run/docker.sock
Ninety percent of the time this means the service is not running, or your user is not in the docker group.
★
On Docker Desktop (Mac/Windows) there is no systemctl — you start and stop Docker from the Desktop application instead.

Two ways to write the same command

The object word is optional for the common commands — Docker infers it.

The modern, explicit form
bash
docker container run -it ubuntu
docker image build .
ⓘ
Says exactly which object you are acting on. Clearer in scripts and in documentation, and it matches the grammar on the previous slide one-to-one.
The older shorthand
bash
docker run -it ubuntu
docker build .
★
Same result. Shorter to type, and what you will see in most tutorials and Stack Overflow answers. Both are correct.

docker pull — get an image locally

bash

Why pull separately? You get a specific version (tag) on your machine before you run anything. On a slow or unreliable network, pulling once and then running avoids surprises mid-demo.

docker run — foreground

The simplest possible run: attached to your terminal, gone when you stop it.

bash
docker run --rm nginx:1.25-alpine
What happens
  • Logs stream straight into your terminal.
  • Your prompt is blocked until the container stops.
  • Stop it with Ctrl+C.
The flag
★
--rm deletes the container as soon as it stops. It keeps your machine tidy while practising — no pile of exited containers to clean up later.
ⓘ
This mode is for quick tests and one-off commands. For anything that should keep running, use detached mode on the next slide.

This single line is the shape of almost every real container you will ever start.

-dDetached — runs in the background and returns your prompt

The container lifecycle

Exited is not removed. A stopped container still exists, still holds its writable layer, and still shows up in docker ps -a.

Docker · ITI DevOps 202638 / 140
4 · CLI

Lifecycle without losing the container

Create, then start later
bash
docker container create httpd
bash
docker container start 36a391532e10
ⓘ
create prepares the container and prints its ID, but starts nothing. Useful when you want to configure first and launch later.
Stop and start an existing container
bash
docker stop web
bash
docker start web
★
The container keeps its writable layer — files it wrote are still there when it starts again.
⚠
run vs start The contrast that matters: docker run = create a new container + start it. docker start = start an existing one. Running docker run five times leaves you with five containers.
Docker · ITI DevOps 202639 / 140
4 · CLI

docker logs — stdout and stderr

bash
docker logs web
docker logs -f web    # follow (like tail -f)
Why this is your first tool
  • It is usually the fastest way to see crashes, bad config, and stack traces.
  • -f follows the stream live — leave it open in a second terminal while you test.
  • Works on stopped containers too, which is exactly when you need it most.
bash
docker container logs logtest
docker container logs -f logtest
⚠
Important Docker captures whatever the main process writes to stdout and stderr. If your app logs to a file inside the container instead, docker logs shows nothing — that is a common surprise.
Docker · ITI DevOps 202640 / 140
4 · CLI

docker exec — a shell inside a running container

bash
docker exec -it web sh
# inside: ls /usr/share/nginx/html
# exit with: exit
Why it is so useful
?
The shell inside the container sees that filesystem and that network. It answers the question “what does the app actually see?” — which is almost always different from what you assumed.
The two flags
FlagMeaning
-iInteractive — keep stdin open
-tAllocate a TTY — gives you a real prompt
-itThe two together. What you will always type.
You can also address a container by ID
bash
docker container exec -it b71f15d33b60 /bin/bash
ⓘ
Careful Which shell you ask for matters — and it depends on the base image. That is the next slide.

4 · CLI

Which shell? It depends on the base image

>_ Alpine
alpine · nginx:alpine · node:20-alpine
  • Small image — a few MB
  • Uses /bin/sh (BusyBox ash)
  • No bash by default
bash
docker exec -it web sh
>_ Debian / Ubuntu
ubuntu · debian · python:3.9-slim
  • Larger image — tens to hundreds of MB
  • Includes bash
  • Can also use sh
bash
docker exec -it web bash
★
The rule Ask for bash on an Alpine image and you get “exec: bash: executable file not found”. When in doubt, try sh — every image has it.

4 · CLI

attach vs exec — a classic trap

Use exec almost always. Reach for attach only when you genuinely need the main process’s console.

attach — connect to the MAIN process
bash
docker container attach ubuntu
ⓘ
Attaches your terminal to the container’s existing PID 1 — the same stdin/stdout the container already had. You are not starting anything new.
⚠
The trap: pressing Ctrl+C here sends SIGINT to PID 1 and stops the container. Detach safely with Ctrl+P then Ctrl+Q instead.
exec — start a NEW process
bash
docker container exec -it ubuntu bash
ⓘ
Starts a second, independent process inside the running container. Exiting the shell leaves the container untouched.
★
If a container is stuck and will not stop, this is the blunt instrument:
bash
docker container kill ubuntu
Docker · ITI DevOps 202643 / 140

docker inspect — the full JSON truth

bash
docker inspect web
bash
docker inspect -f '{{range.NetworkSettings.Networks}}{{.IPAddress}}{{end}}' web
What you get
  • IP addresses, mounts, environment variables, restart policy, entrypoint, labels, health status.
  • Everything docker ps is too narrow to show.
The -f / --format flag
★
Raw inspect output is hundreds of lines of JSON. -f takes a Go template and extracts one value — perfect for scripts and for the networking labs coming up.
bash
docker container inspect webapp

Linux signals vs Docker commands

Docker’s lifecycle verbs are thin wrappers over ordinary Unix signals.

On a normal Linux processThe Docker equivalent
kill -SIGSTOP $(pgrep httpd)SIGSTOPdocker container pause web
kill -SIGCONT $(pgrep httpd)SIGCONTdocker container unpause web
kill -SIGTERM $(pgrep httpd)SIGTERMdocker container stop web
kill -SIGKILL $(pgrep httpd)SIGKILLdocker container kill web
⚠
The difference that matters stop is polite, kill is not. stop sends SIGTERM and waits (10s by default) for the app to shut down cleanly, then sends SIGKILL. kill sends SIGKILL immediately — no cleanup, no flushing, possible data loss.

The --rm flag and one-off containers

What just happened
  1. 1
    Docker started an Ubuntu container.
  2. 2
    It ran expr 4 + 5, which printed 9.
  3. 3
    The command finished, so the container exited.
  4. 4
    --rm deleted it immediately — nothing left behind.
?
The rule A container lives exactly as long as its main process. When that process exits, the container stops. There is no such thing as an “empty running container”.

Restart policies

bash

PolicyBehaviour
noDefault. Never restart automatically.
on-failure[:n]Restart only if the container exits with a non-zero code. Optionally cap the attempts.
alwaysAlways restart — including after the Docker daemon restarts or the host reboots.
unless-stoppedLike always, except it stays down if you stopped it manually. Usually what you want.
⚠
Restart policies are the reason a container can come back after a reboot without any systemd unit. They are also the reason a broken container can loop forever — check docker ps -a for a climbing restart count.

Publishing a port: -p host:container

bash
docker run -d --name web -p 8080:80 nginx:1.25-alpine
-p 8080:80
8080 — host
Left side. The port on your machine — what you type in the URL: localhost:8080. You choose this freely.
80 — container
Right side. The port the app listens on inside the container. Decided by the image, not by you.
★
Traffic hits the host on 8080 → Docker forwards it → the container receives it on 80. Change the left number freely; the right number must match what the app actually listens on.

5 · Networking

Port mapping in practice

Lowercase -p is explicit. Uppercase -P is automatic and random.

bash
docker run -p 80:5000 kodekloud/simple-webapp
ⓘ
Host 80 → container 5000. Reachable at plain http://localhost — no port in the URL.
bash
docker run -p 8000:5000 kodekloud/simple-webapp
ⓘ
Same image, different host port. Run both at once — two containers, two host ports, no conflict.
bash
docker run -p 3306:3306 mysql
ⓘ
Databases work the same way. Now mysql -h 127.0.0.1 on the host reaches the container.
bash
docker run -P --expose=8080 kodekloud/simple-webapp
★
Capital -P publishes all exposed ports to random high host ports. Find them with docker ps.
⚠
Guaranteed error Two containers cannot share one host port. -p 8080:80 twice fails with “port is already allocated” — change the left number.

5 · Networking

The mistake everyone makes once: 127.0.0.1 vs 0.0.0.0

The symptom
⚠
The port mapping looks correct, docker ps shows 0.0.0.0:8080->80/tcp, and the browser still says connection reset.
The cause

The app inside the container is bound to 127.0.0.1 — the container’s own loopback. Docker forwards traffic to the container’s eth0 address, which the app is not listening on. The packet arrives and is refused.

The fix

Bind the app to 0.0.0.0 — all interfaces — whenever it must accept connections from outside the container.

Bind addressReachable from
127.0.0.1Only inside that container
0.0.0.0The host via -p, and other containers
★
You saw this already in our Flask lab app: app.run(host="0.0.0.0", port=5000). That host= argument is exactly this fix.
Docker · ITI DevOps 202662 / 140
5 · Networking

Network drivers

ⓘ
Docker connects containers using network drivers. This course focuses on three: bridge (default and user-defined), host, and none. Others exist — for example overlay for Swarm and Kubernetes — but they are out of scope here.
DriverWhat it doesTypical use
bridgeContainers sit on a Linux bridge with NAT to the outside (unless the network is --internal). User-defined bridges add automatic DNS between containers on that network.Almost all app containers
hostThe container shares the host’s network stack. There are no separately published ports in the usual sense on Linux — what you bind on port 80 is the host’s port 80.Very low latency or legacy apps. Less isolation.
noneOnly the loopback interface inside the container — no external network at all.Jobs that must not touch the network

5 · Networking

The default bridge: reachable by IP, not by name

This single limitation is the reason user-defined networks exist.

ⓘ
New containers attach to Docker’s default bridge (called bridge in docker network ls) unless you pass --network.
BehaviourOn the default bridge
Container ↔ containerThey can talk using each other’s container IP (e.g. 172.17.x.x). Find them with docker inspect <name>.
DNS by container nameNo. The embedded DNS server that maps names → containers does not apply on the default bridge the way it does on a user-defined bridge. http://other-container usually fails unless you add manual host entries.
Host vs containerContainers are not on the host’s LAN as regular NICs. They sit behind Docker’s bridge and NAT. They are logically isolated from the host’s network namespace, even though traffic can route out through the host.

5 · Networking

User-defined bridges: you get DNS

This is the single most useful networking fact in Docker. Create a network, name your containers, call them by name.

The default bridge
curl http://api  ✗

No embedded DNS for container names. You need the IP, or a manual --add-host entry that goes stale.

A user-defined bridge
curl http://api  ✓

The container’s --name becomes a hostname for every other container on that same network. Docker’s embedded DNS resolves it, and it keeps working after a restart.

Create one and use it
bash
docker network ls
docker network create mynet
docker run -d --name app --network mynet nginx:1.25-alpine
docker run --rm --network mynet curlimages/curl curl -s http://app
★
On mynet, the name app resolves to that container. Simple service discovery — no Kubernetes required.

EXPECTED TO FAILTry to reach the internet from an --internal network

PatternWhen to use itExample

Named volume vs bind mount

Same -v flag, two very different behaviours. The left side of the colon tells you which one you got.

Named volume
docker manages the storage
Container  /var/lib/mysql
↕  mounted by name
Volume  mysql-docker-data
docker stores it under
/var/lib/docker/volumes/…

You refer to it by name. You never type a host path, and you do not care where Docker actually put it.

Bind mount
you choose an exact host path
Container  /app
↕  mounted by path
Host  $PWD/app
a real folder you can
open in your editor

You point at a directory on your machine. Edit a file in your editor and the container sees the change instantly — no rebuild.

  • Perfect for live-editing source code
  • Easy to inspect and back up by hand

6 · Volumes

Stateless vs stateful applications

Design your app to be stateless wherever you can, and be deliberate about the parts that cannot be.

Stateless

Keeps no important local data. Every instance is interchangeable, and you can kill or replace one at any moment without consequence.

web front-endsREST APIsworkersnginxCI jobs
★
Scale by adding more copies. No volumes needed — this is the easy case, and it is what containers were designed for.
Stateful

Owns data that must survive a restart, a redeploy, or the container being deleted. Instances are not interchangeable.

MySQL / PostgresRedis (persisted)MongoDBfile uploadsmessage queues
⚠
Always needs a volume. Scaling is harder because the data has to go somewhere specific — this is why databases were the last thing teams moved into containers.

7 · Dockerfile

Instructions, part 1 — the base and the filesystem

These seven build the filesystem. The next slide covers how the container runs.

InstructionRole
FROMSets the base image and starts a build stage. Every Dockerfile begins with it. Use tags (node:20-alpine) or digests for reproducible builds.
WORKDIRSets the current directory for later RUN, CMD, ENTRYPOINT and COPY. Prefer it over cd inside a RUN.
COPYCopies files from the build context into the image. This is what you use for source code and config.
ADDLike COPY, but can also fetch URLs and auto-extract local tar archives. For most projects COPY is enough and easier to reason about.
RUNRuns a command while building — install packages, compile, npm ci. Each RUN can create a new layer; chaining commands in one RUN reduces layer count when that helps.
ENVSets environment variables inside the image — available at build time and when the container runs.
ARGBuild-time variables (e.g. version pins). Not kept in the final image unless referenced by ENV. Used with docker build --build-arg.
Docker · ITI DevOps 202697 / 140
7 · Dockerfile

Instructions, part 2 — how the container runs

EXPOSE documents. -p publishes. They are not the same thing.

InstructionRole
EXPOSEDocuments which ports the app uses. It does not publish anything by itself — you still need -p on docker run (or Compose).
CMDThe default command when a container starts. docker run myimage node other.js overrides it. Prefer exec form ["node", "server.js"] so signals reach your process.
ENTRYPOINTDefines the main executable; CMD then supplies default arguments. Good for wrapping a binary — combine carefully with docker run argument rules.
USERRuns later RUN/CMD as a non-root user. Better security — create the user in the image first.
VOLUMEDeclares a mount point for persistent or shared data. Documents intent, and creates an anonymous volume if nothing is mounted at run time.
HEALTHCHECKTells Docker how to test whether the app inside is still healthy. Common in production Compose and Kubernetes setups.

7 · Dockerfile

Exec form vs shell form

This connects straight back to the signals slide: exec form is why graceful shutdown works.

Exec form — prefer this
Dockerfile
RUN ["npm", "ci"]
CMD ["node", "app.js"]

No shell wrapper. Your process becomes PID 1 and receives signals directly — so docker stop can shut it down gracefully.

★
Always use exec form for CMD and ENTRYPOINT.
Shell form
Dockerfile
RUN npm ci
CMD node app.js

Runs through /bin/sh -c. The shell is PID 1, your app is a child — and SIGTERM never reaches it. docker stop waits 10 seconds, then SIGKILLs.

ⓘ
Fine for RUN, where you often want shell features like && and variable expansion.

ENTRYPOINT FLASK_APP=/opt/source-code/app.py flask run

docker build . -t my-custom-app
What to notice
  • It starts FROM a base image and layers changes on top — this is the whole idea.
  • Each RUN creates another layer. Four RUN lines here where one would do.
  • COPY . /opt/source-code brings the app in from the build context.
  • ENTRYPOINT in shell form — so this app will not receive SIGTERM cleanly.
ⓘ

A production-shaped single-stage build

Node.js — install then run
Dockerfile

WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
Build and run it
bash

docker run --rm -p 3000:3000 myapp:1.0
Why the lines are in that order
  1. 1
    Pinned base tag — node:20-alpine, not node:latest.
  2. 2
    COPY package*.json before the source code.
  3. 3
    RUN npm ci — the slow step, now in its own layer.
  4. 4
    COPY . . — the code, which changes constantly, comes last.
  5. 5
    Exec-form CMD so the app is PID 1.

The ordering trick Steps 2–4 are the single most valuable Dockerfile habit: change the cheap things last. Edit your source and the expensive npm ci layer is still cached.

7 · Dockerfile

How the build cache actually works

You edited one line of source code, then rebuilt
CACHED FROM node:20-alpine
CACHED WORKDIR /app
CACHED COPY package*.json ./
CACHED RUN npm ci  ← 90s saved
CHANGED COPY . .  ← your edit
REBUILT EXPOSE 3000
REBUILT CMD ["node", "server.js"]
The rule
?
Cache invalidation Docker walks the instructions top to bottom. It reuses the cached layer for each one until it hits a change — then every instruction after that point is rebuilt, cached or not.
★
So put the instructions that rarely change at the top, and the ones that change on every commit at the bottom. That is the entire optimisation.
ⓘ
This is also why COPY package*.json ./ and RUN npm ci come before COPY . . — dependencies change weekly, source changes hourly.
Docker · ITI DevOps 2026102 / 140
7 · Dockerfile

Cache busting and version pinning

Two opposite problems: the cache being too sticky, and tags being too loose.

Cache busting

Sometimes the cache works against you. RUN apt-get update can be cached for weeks, so a later install pulls a stale package index.

Fix: chain them in a single RUN so they always invalidate together.

Dockerfile
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl
Version pinning

An unpinned tag makes builds non-reproducible. The same Dockerfile can produce different images on different days.

Pin the base image, and pin package versions where it matters.

Dockerfile
FROM node:20.11-alpine        # not node:latest
RUN pip install flask==3.0.0  # not just flask

Security An image is not a secret store. Anything you COPY in stays in that layer forever — deleting it in a later layer does not remove it from the image.

7 · Dockerfile

Multi-stage builds: the idea

Smaller images, faster deploys, less attack surface, and a clean separation between “build” and “run”.

Stage 1 — build
FROM golang:1.22-alpine AS builder
  • Full compiler toolchain
  • Dev dependencies
  • Source code and tests
  • Produces one binary
~350 MBthrown away
⟶
COPY --from=builder
copies only the artifact
Stage 2 — runtime
FROM alpine:3.19
  • Tiny base image
  • No compiler, no SDK
  • No source code
  • Just the binary
~15 MBthis is what you ship
?
Each FROM starts a new stage. AS name labels a stage. COPY --from=stage copies artifacts from an earlier stage into the current one. Everything else in the build stage is discarded.
Docker · ITI DevOps 2026105 / 140
7 · Dockerfile

Multi-stage Go — stage 1: the builder

The build stage
Dockerfile
# --- build stage: full Go toolchain ---
FROM golang:1.22-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /src

COPY go.mod go.sum ./
RUN go mod download

COPY . .
# static binary, no C linker dependency in final image
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -ldflags="-s -w" -o /out/server .
Line by line
  • AS builder names this stage so the next one can copy from it.
  • COPY go.mod go.sum then go mod download — the same cache trick as package*.json: dependencies before source.
  • -ldflags="-s -w" strips debug symbols, shrinking the binary.
  • The binary is written to /out/server, a path the next stage will reach for.
?
Why CGO_ENABLED=0? It usually produces a fully static binary, so you do not need C libraries in the final image. Whether it does depends on your code and dependencies.
Docker · ITI DevOps 2026106 / 140
7 · Dockerfile

Multi-stage Go — stage 2: the runtime

The runtime stage (same file, continued)
Dockerfile
# --- runtime stage: tiny base, no Go SDK ---
FROM alpine:3.19
WORKDIR /app

RUN adduser -D appuser

COPY --from=builder /out/server ./server
USER appuser

EXPOSE 8080
CMD ["./server"]
Build and run (adjust the port to match your app)
bash
docker build -t mygoapp:1.0 .
docker run --rm -p 8080:8080 mygoapp:1.0
What changed
  • A second FROM — everything from the builder stage is now discarded.
  • RUN adduser -D appuser then USER appuser — the container no longer runs as root.
  • COPY --from=builder reaches into stage 1 and takes only the binary.
  • No Go, no gcc, no source code in the shipped image.
★
The USER line is free security. If an attacker gets code execution, they land as an unprivileged user instead of root.
Docker · ITI DevOps 2026107 / 140
7 · Dockerfile

Multi-stage Node — deps and build stages

Stages 1 and 2
Dockerfile
# --- dependencies ---
FROM node:20-alpine AS deps
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci

# --- build (compile/bundle) ---
FROM node:20-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=deps /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY . .
RUN npm run build
The pattern
  • deps — install everything, including dev dependencies, in an isolated stage.
  • build — reuse those node_modules, add the source, and run the bundler or TypeScript compiler.
  • Splitting them means a source-only change does not reinstall dependencies.
ⓘ
Three stages One stage for dependencies, one for build, one for production. The third stage is on the next slide.

7 · Dockerfile

Multi-stage Node — the production stage

Stage 3 (same file, continued)
Dockerfile
# --- production runtime ---
FROM node:20-alpine AS prod
WORKDIR /app
ENV NODE_ENV=production

COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev && npm cache clean --force

COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist

EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]

What ships
  • npm ci --omit=dev — production dependencies only. No test frameworks, no bundlers.
  • COPY --from=build /app/dist — only the compiled output, never the source.
  • npm cache clean --force keeps the npm cache out of the layer.
★
Adjust the paths (dist/server.js, npm run build) to match your project. With no build step you only need two stages: deps and prod copying source and running npm ci --omit=dev.

--target stops the build at a named stage — useful to build just build in CI to run tests.

Part 7 recap

Habits worth keeping
  • Use the official Dockerfile reference for every instruction and edge case.
  • Single-stage is simplest; multi-stage is standard for production Go, Node, Java and Rust.

  • Use CMD in exec form; use EXPOSE as documentation and publish ports with docker run -p.

  • Always add a .dockerignore. Always pin your base tag.

8 · Compose

Why Compose?

One file can start several containers with their networks and volumes — much closer to a real project.

Without Compose
docker network create app-net
docker volume create pgdata
docker run -d --name db --network app-net -v pgdata:/var/lib/…
docker run -d --name redis --network app-net redis:alpine
docker run -d --name api --network app-net -p 5000:5000 …
docker run -d --name worker --network app-net myorg/worker
⚠
Six commands, in the right order, with the right flags — retyped by every developer, on every machine, every time. Nothing is written down except in shell history.
With Compose
bash
docker compose up -d
★
One command. The file next to it records every port, volume, environment variable and dependency. It lives in Git, gets reviewed in pull requests, and works identically on everyone’s laptop.
?
Compose also creates a user-defined network for you automatically — which is why services can reach each other by service name with no extra configuration. That is the DNS lesson from part 5, applied.

Lab 13 · Step 2

Fix the port conflict first

⚠
Read this before you run it The compose file publishes the vote app on host port 5000. On macOS that port is normally already taken by AirPlay Receiver, and the vote container will refuse to start:
error
Error response from daemon: Ports are not available: listen tcp 0.0.0.0:5000: bind: address already in use
2 · Create an override file that moves the ports
docker-compose.override.yml
cat > docker-compose.override.yml <<'EOF'
services:
  vote:
    ports: !override ["5050:80"]
  result:
    ports: !override ["5051:80"]
EOF
?
Why !override Compose merges docker-compose.override.yml automatically. !override replaces the ports list — without it Compose appends, so the container would still try to bind 5000 and still fail.

8 · Compose

Part 8 recap

What Compose gives you
  • One declarative file for many containers, in version control.
  • An automatic user-defined network — services reach each other by name.
  • Named volumes, environment variables, ports and build settings all written down.
  • The same project starts identically on every machine.
The commands
CommandPurpose
docker compose up -dBuild, create and start everything
docker compose up --buildForce a rebuild first
docker compose psStatus of this project
docker compose logs -fFollow all service logs
docker compose exec svc shShell into a service
docker compose downStop and remove containers + network
docker compose down -vAlso delete volumes (data loss)

9 · Debugging

When a container misbehaves, work in this order

Do not guess. Go down the list — it is ordered by how often the answer is there.

  1. 1
    docker ps -a — Is it running at all? What was the exit code? Exit 0 means it finished; 137 means SIGKILL (often out of memory); 1 means the app errored.
  2. 2
    docker logs <name> — Did it crash on startup? This catches the majority of problems in one step.
  3. 3
    docker inspect <name> — Wrong environment variables? Wrong command? Wrong mounts? The config you thought you passed may not be what it got.
  4. 4
    docker exec -it <name> sh — Can you see the right files? Does DNS resolve? Can you curl the dependencies from in there?
  5. 5
    Ports — Is the -p mapping correct, and is the app listening on 0.0.0.0 rather than 127.0.0.1?
  6. 6
    Volumes — Is the data where you expect it? Any permission errors in the logs?
Docker · ITI DevOps 2026132 / 140
9 · Debugging

When the daemon is the problem

Read the service logs
bash
journalctl -u docker.service
ⓘ
systemd’s log for dockerd itself. Where you look when Docker will not start, or dies unexpectedly.
Ask the daemon about itself
bash
docker system info
ⓘ
Storage driver, cgroup version, warnings, registry mirrors. Also prints Debug Mode status.
The daemon configuration file
path
/etc/docker/daemon.json
★
Where you set the default logging driver, registry mirrors, storage driver, debug mode and live restore. Edit it, then systemctl restart docker to apply.
Docker · ITI DevOps 2026133 / 140
9 · Debugging

Logging drivers and live restore

Logging drivers
bash
docker run -d --log-driver json-file nginx
DriverWhere logs go
json-fileLocal JSON files — the default. What docker logs reads.
localLocal, more efficient binary format
syslog / journaldThe host’s system logger
awslogs, gelf, fluentdShip straight to a central log platform
⚠
With a remote driver, docker logs may return nothing — the logs went elsewhere. Expected, and confusing the first time.
Live restore

Normally, restarting the Docker daemon stops your containers. Live restore lets them keep running while dockerd restarts or upgrades.

/etc/docker/daemon.json
{
  "live-restore": true
}
?
This is what the containerd-shim from part 3 makes possible — each container has its own supervising process that does not depend on the daemon being alive.
ⓘ
Not compatible with Swarm mode, and it only covers daemon restarts — not a host reboot. For reboots you want a restart policy.

Glossary

The vocabulary you now share with every DevOps team.

ImageImmutable template made of layers.
ContainerA runnable instance of an image.
RegistryImage storage — Docker Hub, ECR, GHCR…
TagA label for an image version, e.g. :1.25-alpine.
LayerA reusable filesystem diff inside an image.
VolumePersistent storage outside the container’s thin writable layer.
Port publishMap a host port to a container port with -p.
Build contextThe directory sent to the daemon for docker build.
Bind mountA host directory mounted into a container.
NamespaceKernel feature isolating what a process can see.
cgroupKernel feature limiting what a process can use.
Multi-stageA build where only the artifacts reach the final image.

9 · Recap

The whole picture

▤

Images

Immutable, layered, pulled from a registry or built from a Dockerfile.

◉

Containers

Isolated processes with a thin writable layer. Created, started, stopped, removed.

⇄

Networks

Publish ports for the host. Use a user-defined bridge so containers find each other by name.

◫

Volumes

The only place data survives. Named volumes for data, bind mounts for dev.

application
